revision.author: 0x8432319097D7365a686167Bab33d7425B356b2b2
revision.title: EEZ Extends Ethereum: Making Its Contracts Safe for Chains to Adopt
revision.summary:
EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it. 

A Layer 2 stops being an isolated network behind a bridge, and a protocol deploys once instead of maintaining copies on every chain. This initiative funds the independent security audit of this Ethereum public good through TheDAO Security Fund. Gnosis separately funds a public Verification Sandbox where chain teams verify the audited contracts against their own stack. A public audit record, and a final milestone that pays only when external chains publish real verification results on the audited contracts.

sections.why:
**EEZ extends Ethereum, and Ethereum's security with it.** Some of the largest losses in Ethereum's history happened at its bridges: honeypots of locked funds guarded by small signer sets, most of them relying on reputation rather than contract logic or validity proofs, prioritizing UX over security, and that signer set becomes the security ceiling for every user behind it. The record shows it: the largest exploits in crypto's history are dominated by bridge signer and verifier compromises, Ronin, Poly Network, BNB Bridge, Wormhole, Nomad among them ([Rekt leaderboard](https://rekt.news/leaderboard/)). Async messages add a second problem: a transfer can get stuck halfway, and most cross-chain bugs live in that halfway state. EEZ ends both by making every Layer 2 a true extension of Ethereum instead of an isolated network behind a bridge: one account works everywhere, a contract keeps one address, and a cross-chain action either completes fully or does not happen at all. EEZ is able to achieve both: it maintains the exact security guarantees specified by the network, and it improves the UX of current reputation-based bridges. Securing the EEZ contracts is a security upgrade to Ethereum itself.

The clearest win is a smaller attack surface. Today a protocol deploys a copy of itself on every network it wants to reach, and duplication breeds bugs: version drift, per-chain initialization mistakes, maintenance across every copy. The Balancer v2 exploit drained the same duplicated code chain by chain. With EEZ a protocol can deploy once, on the network where it is easiest to control, audit, and secure, and every chain uses it through atomic cross-chain communication. One deployment, one audit, one patch, effective everywhere.

Concentration cuts both ways, and that is exactly why this audit is a shared responsibility. EEZ cannot weaken Ethereum L1 itself consensus does not depend on it. But every chain that adopts EEZ routes its cross-chain security through one contract set on Ethereum. A critical bug there would not be one chain's incident; it would be every connected chain's incident at once. The same design that removes per-bridge honeypots replaces many weak surfaces with one surface that must be strong. Infrastructure with a shared failure domain deserves shared, independent scrutiny before chains adopt it which is what this initiative funds. Shared risk requires shared security and shared funding.

How EEZ changes where security comes from:

- **Chosen by the chain, enforced on L1.** Each rollup declares the proof systems it accepts and the threshold that must agree, and every cross-chain action settles against that verification on Ethereum, designed for one aggregated proof per proof system per L1 block. Security is not bought with speed: a chain keeps the properties it chooses without giving up the UX of an instant call. Rollups that run based, like the first Gnosis deployment, go further: sequencing happens inside the L1 block itself, and anyone can rebuild the full chain from L1 data alone.
- **No half-done state.** A cross-chain call and its return value execute in one transaction. Everything commits or nothing does, so stuck funds and partial-state exploits are removed by design.
- **Verified, not trusted.** Every cross-chain outcome is precomputed and checked on L1 against the proof systems the rollup declared. Today that check is a single attestation signer re-executing the block window; the multi-prover design it plugs into is described below. A malicious operator cannot forge a result, only fail to produce one.
    - **No single proof system to break, by design.** With multiple proof systems and a threshold, one prover's bug does not compromise the chain. Verifying the live attestation pipeline, and the multi-prover design it plugs into, is in this audit's scope.

For users, this also means wallets can automate cross-chain sends, so funds sent to the right address on the wrong chain stop being a loss.

EEZ is not a dapp and not a product. It is an Ethereum public good: an open, permissionless protocol and  infrastructure for synchronous composability between Ethereum rollups. The core EEZ contract has no admin role. Each connected rollup keeps its own contract, whose owner sets the accepted proof systems, verification keys, and threshold; reviewing those privileged roles and how they can be locked down is part of this audit . EEZ is FOSS and has no token. That design puts the security of the whole system on its smart contracts, which is exactly what this initiative puts under independent review. The contracts are deployed on testnets and ready for audit.

The adoption signals are already public. GnosisDAO has approved GIP-153, making Gnosis Chain the first governance-backed adopter. Celo, Polygon, and Linea have stated they will test the audited contracts once the audit completes. 

Joseph Lubin has publicly spoken in support of the Ethereum Economic Zone ([post](https://x.com/etheconomiczone/status/2052390993610133513)). Every team in these conversations asks for the same thing first: an independent security record.

The design has been stress-tested in public. At ETHPrague 2026, Vitalik Buterin probed the worst case with Jordi Baylina, one chain's proof system breaking, and the answer held: damage stays confined to contracts that chose to trust the broken chain; users everywhere else are untouched ([fireside](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=prgWmgUbSVQ)). At Dappcon Berlin, Buterin named the risk EEZ prevents, interoperability "captured by centralized providers," and called EEZ "a quite helpful effort in that regard"([panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gfG-R8AOu0E)).
sections.in_scope:
**Expected Audit Process**

We expect the audit engagement to follow a clear and structured process, completed within 2 months of auditor selection. Selection follows TheDAO's process: full funding, a 30-day proposal window, then a 7-day decision. With funding closed by late October 2026, the report lands by late January 2027, leaving roughly ten weeks of the 6-month duration for the adoption milestone. That window is tight, which is why adoption criterion 1 carries a testnet fallback. The audit budget corresponds to 8 to 10 senior-auditor-weeks at prevailing protocol-audit rates plus remediation review; competitive bidding is the price check.

**1. Scope & Kick-off**

Confirm the exact codebase, commit hash, components in scope, relevant dependencies, assumptions, and known areas of concern.

**2. System Understanding**

Review the protocol architecture, critical flows, privileged roles, trust assumptions, and key security properties before starting the detailed review. Understand how protocol messages, proof commitments, and execution on Ethereum L1 and participating rollups (L2s) fit together.

**3. Security Review**

Perform an independent manual review of the in-scope code and protocol documentation, supported by appropriate security tooling and testing techniques where relevant. Cross-chain behavior is a required part of this review.

In addition to contract security, assess:

Whether the contracts match the protocol specification, and the specification is sufficient for independent implementation.

Whether EEZ delivers the intended synchronous cross-chain interactions (nested calls, static reads, failures, rollback) for EVM rollups, and under which assumptions. Non-EVM integration is a design question for the Verification Sandbox, not an audit deliverable.

**4. Findings & Preliminary Report**

Document validated findings with clear severity, impact, root cause, affected components, and recommended remediation. Critical issues should be communicated as soon as they are confirmed.

**5. Findings Review**

Walk through the findings with the development team to align on impact, assumptions, and the proposed remediation approach.

**6. Remediation Review**

Review the implemented fixes and verify that each issue has been properly addressed without introducing regressions.

**7. Final Report**

Deliver a final report covering the audited scope, methodology, findings, remediation status, remaining risks, and the final reviewed code version.

**Verification Sandbox (funded and operated by Gnosis and the EEZ core team, outside this goal)**

Operated by the EEZ core team alongside the audit. Gnosis carries these fixed costs because it is the first adopter and the infrastructure serves its own deployment anyway:

- A persistent public testnet running the audited contracts at the pinned commit or a documented successor
- A published conformance suite any chain can run against its own stack, with integration documentation
- A public intake process for chains that want to test
- External chain engineers invited to comment on the audit's invariant list, so the suite checks what integrators actually need
- The EEZ core team commits in writing that the sandbox stays publicly accessible, with its conformance suite and documentation published, for at least 6 months after the audit report ships

sections.out_scope:
- Rollup node software, provers, sequencers, and any off-chain infrastructure
- The internal economics of individual rollups connected to EEZ
- Re-auditing protocol changes made after the pinned commit
- Marketing, badges, or any public claim beyond what the published evidence supports
sections.existing:
- The protocol source and its contract-level specifications are public: [eez-core-protocol](https://github.com/eez-association/eez-core-protocol), including specs for the core protocol, execution entries, the multi-prover design, and blob format under `docs/`.
- The repository tracks open security findings from internal review. Bidders start from a documented codebase, not a blank page.
sections.who:
Nobody is pre-selected. The winning bid comes from a security firm or audit team with published audits of live mainnet protocols. A consortium is welcome, as long as the auditing team meets the independence requirement in the hard requirements. The audit is the competitive scope of this RFP; the Verification Sandbox is funded by Gnosis and operated by the EEZ core team. Bids price the Full Audit milestone. The adoption evidence milestone is a holdback, not payment for work. It is claimed by the EEZ core team under the same grant agreement and judged by the same independent reviewer, and it pays only when the public evidence listed below exists. To be explicit: the second recipient is the proposer. TheDAO pays the EEZ core team for the holdback only when the public evidence exists; if it never does, the funds return to TheDAO under the 21-day rule. Gnosis funds the Verification Sandbox and the engineering behind it; if no chain publishes, TheDAO pays nothing.

To help Giveth judge the strongest bid, EEZ core contributors Eduardo Antuña and Jesús Ligero will be available as technical advisors during the selection process: they know the codebase best and can assess whether a proposed plan actually covers it.
sections.hard_req:
1. **Everything published.** The full audit report, findings, severity ratings, and fix reviews are released publicly; any test suites or tooling produced ship under an OSI license.
2. **Independent auditor.** The audit team has no shared ownership, personnel, or financial ties to the EEZ core contributors or to Gnosis, disclosed in writing.
3. **Verifiable acceptance.** Every milestone criterion below can be checked by a stranger from public evidence.
4. **Fixed target.** All work runs against one pinned commit. Any material protocol change during the engagement is documented in the public record.

milestones.name: Full Audit
criteria: A pinned commit of eez-core-protocol named as the review target, with the in-scope contract list and the invariant list published for public comment
At least one full independent review of the in-scope contracts completed by an audit team meeting the independence requirement
Complete report published: findings, severity ratings, and status
Every critical and high finding fixed or publicly acknowledged with rationale, and the fixes re-reviewed by the team that found them

milestones.name: Adoption evidence
criteria: The EEZ contracts deployed on Gnosis Chain mainnet under GIP-153 at the audited commit, or a successor documented in the security record, with every critical and high finding resolved, and processing cross-rollup transactions, verifiable on a public block explorer. If Gnosis Chain mainnet under GIP-153 has not launched by the end of the grant duration, this criterion is met by the audited contracts running on the Gnosis public testnet at the audited commit for at least 60 days, with the mainnet date stated in the security record

At least 2 external chain teams, not affiliated with Gnosis or the EEZ core contributors, have run the audited contracts against their own stack and published the result in a form a stranger can check: conformance suite output, a public testnet deployment connecting their chain, or a signed security assessment
